title: DEC-3, the mode is detected, not chosen: `workthread` looks for a running daemon and attaches to it when it finds one; with none running, it executes the work logic in its own process
The daemon is a subcommand of the same binary, meant to be started by a service manager such as systemd, never a second artifact
No first-run wizard, and nothing written to configuration before the first task exists
A lost daemon is not a mode change: while a client is attached and the daemon stops, crashes, or becomes unreachable, the call in flight fails with a clear error; reconnecting or restarting...
Continuing in the client's own process is offered as an explicit action that takes ownership of the data, never as an automatic fallback
DEC-4: a graceful stop records the instant it happened in the operation log and leaves open timers and the session open
On the next start, anything opened before that instant is presented for correction, with its end defaulting to the recorded stop
A crash leaves no fresh stop instant, so the same machinery asks
Consequence for `session-and-timetable`: the `missing_session_end` notice covers a day, and an open time entry needs the same treatment at startup, with the stop instant read from the log...
Configuration has an owner, and no file is shared
The daemon's process configuration, in a file or in the environment, because it has to be readable before the database opens: the data directory, the bind address, the port, the token, and `serveMcp`
The surface's own configuration: an endpoint override for a daemon on another host, and that surface's own preferences such as window size; nothing business-related
The business settings, in the daemon's data: the timetable, the planned start, the break reserve, the four balancing values, the notice levels, the approach lead window, the concurrency setting...
The business settings are all reached through the daemon and its API, never through a file
The API is a contract, not an internal pipe: REST resources organised by record kind, versioned paths, documented with OpenAPI, and usable by consumers outside the application
The remote proxy translates surface-port calls into resource operations, so the split-mode client, the tray, and the CLI all use the same contract, and an external consumer uses what they use
Every operation maps to a resource or to an action on a resource, so there is no RPC-shaped endpoint
The reads that belong together use the change cursor, which the cursor already provides
The live channel is deferred to evidence; v1's API is pull-only: reads with filters and pagination, the change feed by cursor, and notices and confirmations as resources
Whether a live push channel ships at all, and whether it is server-sent events or WebSockets, is decided by two tasks created in this pass: `live-api-research` and then `live-api-choice`
The human's uncertainty is about tooling rather than protocol: Spring's support on the server, OpenAPI's coverage of event streams, AsyncAPI's coverage of WebSockets, and client tooling...
`architecture`: the API module becomes a published contract with an OpenAPI document; the remote proxy maps surface ports onto resources; the daemon/surface configuration split lands here
`decisions-agent-interface`: the REST resources for notices and pending operations have to agree with the MCP tool shapes, since both expose the same state
`session-and-timetable`: an open time entry needs the same startup correction as an unended day
`decisions-data-lifecycle`: the stop instant is written to the operation log, which must therefore record service lifecycle events, not only record changes
`child-efforts`: the API child's scope depends on `live-api-choice`, and the ordering note is recorded there
`live-api-research` and `live-api-choice`: created in this pass, both blocked in order
